Consider the set $A$ shown above. The interior of $A$ is 

$$
\text{int}\,A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<1,\,}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

$$
\text{int}\,A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<1,\,-1<y<0}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge 2-x}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ contains none of its boundary points.
- $A$ contains some (not all) of its boundary points.
- $\text{int}\,A\ne A$
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14041552/assets/cdca164d343d8bff4c78a1e366e52c588ca6c54dfdea61acea1900bcbdc79f31.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

Notice that, in this case, the set $A$ contains all of its boundary points.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statements I and II are false. As we have seen, $A$ contains all its boundary points.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ contains all of its boundary points, we must have $A-∂A⊊A.$ Therefore $\text{int}\,A\ne A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true

questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}<4}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $\text{int}\,A\cap ∂A=∅$
- $A-\text{int}\,A=∂A$
- $∂A⊂{R}^{2}-A$
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14041552/assets/4540e03fc5404474a0cd900c89004e6a5cfe7ac2d4702348e9d0395fc1c914e9.png)

 

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14041552/assets/2a93b912f0d7b3a84bf0ec9c3b3596d080a9e71a345ff436e2f591edf042d9db.png)

  

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement I is true. Since $\text{int}\,A$ contains all points in $A$ except the boundary points, we must have $\text{int}\,A\cap ∂A=∅,$ where $∅$ denotes the empty set.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ contains none of its boundary points, we must have $A=\text{int}\,A$ or, equivalently,  $A-\text{int}\,A=∅.$

- Statement III is true. In this case, the set $A$ contains none of its boundary points, so we must have $∂A⊂{R}^{2}-A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and  III only."

The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $\partial A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $\partial A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14041552/assets/2c7e7ac1b320591250b045ebe493b28e0bb9cdb38469324ee496aacb8766c75b.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\textrm{int}\, A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\textrm{int}\,A = A - \partial A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14041552/assets/49ffc47c2ae1cde5e93e8607db8ef6b58eb7938913f82ea41f281df1fe334c14.png)

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement I is true. Since $\textrm{int}\,A$ contains all points in $A$ except the boundary points, we must have $A - \partial A = \textrm{int}\, A.$

- Statement II is true. Since $\textrm{int}\,A$ contains all points in $A$ except the boundary points, we must have $\textrm{int}\, A \cap \partial A = \emptyset,$ where $\emptyset$ denotes the empty set.

- Statement III is true. In this case, the set $A$ contains all of its boundary points, so we must have $A = \textrm{int}\,A \cup \partial A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
